what-is-terminal.title: What is a Terminal?
what-is-terminal.description: Learn what a terminal is and how it works on Android. This is the foundation for everything you'll learn.

items.title: What is a Terminal?
items.content:
A terminal is a text-based interface for controlling your computer. Instead of clicking buttons with a mouse, you type commands. When you press Enter, the computer executes your command.

Termux brings this same experience to Android. It turns your phone into a mini Linux environment where you can run real commands, install software, write code, and automate tasks — all from a simple text interface.

Think of it this way: while most apps have buttons and menus, Termux is like having a conversation with your phone by typing instructions. It's more powerful but requires learning a few key concepts.
items.example:
{{command}}pwd{{/command}} - Shows your current location in the file system.
{{command}}ls{{/command}} - Lists all files and folders in your current location.
items.exercise: Open Termux and type the word 'hello'. Observe what happens. Then try typing something that you think might be a valid command. Pay attention to the error messages you receive.

items.title: Your First Command
items.content:
Before installing anything, you need to update Termux's list of available apps. This is like refreshing a webpage to get the latest content.

The command you'll run is {{command}}pkg update{{/command}}. pkg is Termux's package manager — it handles installing and updating software. {{command}}update{{/command}} tells it to refresh its list of available packages from the internet.

When you run this, you'll see a lot of text scroll by. This is normal! Termux is downloading the latest information about what software is available to install.

After the update completes, you should also run {{command}}pkg upgrade{{/command}} to install any updates to your existing software. This keeps everything secure and working properly.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg update{{/command}} - Refreshes the package list.
{{command}}pkg upgrade{{/command}} - Installs updates for installed packages.
items.exercise: Run the command to refresh the package list. Then run the command that installs any available updates for your installed software.

items.title: Understanding the Prompt
items.content:
The text before your cursor tells you where you are in the file system. This is called the 'prompt' and it's your guide to navigation.

In Termux, the prompt typically shows your current folder followed by a symbol. ~ means you're in your home folder. $ means you're a regular user (not root).

When you navigate to different folders, the prompt updates to show your new location. This helps you stay oriented as you move around the file system.

Your home folder (represented by ~) is where all your personal files and projects should live. It's your safe space within the file system.
items.example:
{{command}}~ ${{/command}} - You're in your home folder.
{{command}}~/storage ${{/command}} - You're in the storage folder.
items.exercise: Type the command that shows your current location. Then type the command that takes you to the root directory. Type the command that shows your location again to see the change. Finally, go back to your home folder.

how-commands-work.title: How Commands Work
how-commands-work.description: Understand the pattern behind every terminal command. Commands follow a simple structure you can learn once and use forever.

items.title: The Command Pattern
items.content:
Every terminal command follows a simple pattern: COMMAND followed by WHAT TO ACT ON. This is like giving instructions: first the action (verb), then the target (noun).

For example, {{command}}ls Documents{{/command}} means 'list the contents of the Documents folder'. {{command}}cp file.txt backup/{{/command}} means 'copy file.txt to the backup folder'.

Some commands don't need a target. {{command}}ls{{/command}} by itself lists the current folder. {{command}}pwd{{/command}} shows where you are without needing any extra information.

Understanding this pattern makes learning new commands much easier. You'll find that most commands follow this same structure.
items.example:
{{command}}ls{{/command}} - Lists current folder.
{{command}}ls /data{{/command}} - Lists the data folder.
items.exercise: List the contents of your current folder. Then list the contents of the /data folder. Notice how the output changes based on what folder you're looking at.

items.title: Step-by-Step: Navigate Folders
items.content:
Navigation is the most important skill in the terminal. You'll constantly move between folders, check where you are, and see what's inside.

The three essential navigation commands are: {{command}}pwd{{/command}} (where am I?), {{command}}ls{{/command}} (what's here?), and {{command}}cd{{/command}} (go there). Master these and you can navigate anywhere.

When you use {{command}}cd{{/command}}, you can go to a folder by name, go up one level with {{command}}cd ..{{/command}}, or go to your home folder with {{command}}cd ~{{/command}}.

The {{command}}cd ..{{/command}} command is particularly useful — it takes you to the parent folder of your current location. Use it to go back up the folder structure.
items.example:
{{command}}cd ..{{/command}} - Moves up one folder level.
{{command}}cd ~{{/command}} - Goes to your home folder.
items.exercise: Create a new folder. Move into that folder. Create another folder inside it. Check your location. Go back up one level. Check your location again to confirm you moved correctly.

items.title: Making Your First File
items.content:
Creating and editing files is essential. You'll start with simple text files using the Nano editor, which is beginner-friendly.

Nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal. It shows you what you're typing and has basic commands at the bottom of the screen. The most important shortcuts are: Ctrl+O to save and Ctrl+X to exit.

When you create a file with {{command}}touch{{/command}}, it's empty. When you use {{command}}nano{{/command}}, you can actually type content into it. This is how you'll write notes, scripts, and code.

Nano has a learning curve but it's the simplest editor to start with. The commands are shown at the bottom of the screen while you're using it.
items.example:
{{command}}touch mynote.txt{{/command}} - Creates an empty file.
{{command}}nano mynote.txt{{/command}} - Opens it for editing.
items.exercise: Create an empty text file. Open it with the Nano editor. Write a short message about what you're learning. Save your changes and exit. Then view the contents of your file.

essential-commands.title: Essential Commands
essential-commands.description: The most important commands you'll use every day. Memorize these and you'll navigate any terminal with confidence.

items.title: The Three Most Important Commands
items.content:
Memorize these three commands. You will use them constantly in your terminal journey. They are your navigation tools.

{{command}}ls{{/command}} tells you what's in the current folder. {{command}}cd{{/command}} moves you to a different folder. {{command}}pwd{{/command}} tells you exactly where you are.

When you're lost or confused, use these three commands to reorient yourself. {{command}}pwd{{/command}} shows where you are, {{command}}ls{{/command}} shows what's around you, and {{command}}cd{{/command}} takes you where you want to go.
items.example:
{{command}}ls{{/command}} - Lists files.
{{command}}cd /{{/command}} - Goes to root.
{{command}}pwd{{/command}} - Shows current location.
items.exercise: Go to your home folder. List everything there. Go to the root directory. Check your location. Come back to your home folder. Do this sequence 5 times until you can do it without thinking.

items.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
items.content:
Everyone makes mistakes when learning the terminal. Don't feel bad when you see errors — they're part of the learning process.

The most common mistakes are forgetting spaces (commands need spaces between parts), wrong capitalization (Linux is case-sensitive), and typos.

Error messages might look scary but they usually tell you exactly what went wrong. 'command not found' means you typed something that doesn't exist. 'No such file or directory' means the file or folder you mentioned doesn't exist where you are.

Learning to read error messages is a valuable skill. They often contain the exact information you need to fix the problem.
items.example:
{{command}}pwdDocuments{{/command}} - Error: command not found.
{{command}}Ls{{/command}} - Error: command not found.
items.exercise: Try making each of the common mistakes mentioned. Type a command without a space between the command and its argument. Type a command with the wrong capitalization. Type a command that doesn't exist. Read each error message carefully.

items.title: Getting Help
items.content:
When you're stuck, Termux has built-in help systems. You don't need to memorize everything.

Most commands have a {{command}}--help{{/command}} option that shows a quick reference. For more detailed information, you can use the {{command}}man{{/command}} (manual) command.

You can also use the {{command}}history{{/command}} command to see what you've typed before and re-run commands with {{command}}!number{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}ls --help{{/command}} - Shows ls options.
{{command}}man pwd{{/command}} - Shows pwd manual.
items.exercise: View the help page for the ls command. Install the manual pages system. Read the manual for the pwd command. View your command history and re-run a previous command using its number.

mini-project.title: Mini Project
mini-project.description: Put everything together in a real project. Apply all the commands you've learned in a practical scenario.

items.title: Your First Mini Project: A Journal
items.content:
Now you'll put everything together. Create a daily journal to practice all the commands you've learned.

This project uses: {{command}}mkdir{{/command}} to create folders, {{command}}cd{{/command}} to navigate, {{command}}nano{{/command}} to write, {{command}}cat{{/command}} to read, {{command}}cp{{/command}} to backup, and {{command}}ls{{/command}} to check your work.

Start by creating a journal folder, then write your first entry. Make a backup copy to practice the {{command}}cp{{/command}} command. Finally, use {{command}}ls -la{{/command}} to see all the details of your files.
items.example:
{{command}}mkdir journal{{/command}} - Creates journal folder.
{{command}}nano 2026-04-08.txt{{/command}} - Creates and opens entry file.
items.exercise: Create a folder for your journal. Navigate into it. Create a text file with today's date as the name. Write a short entry about what you learned today. Save it and exit. Read your entry. Create a backup copy of your entry. View all files in your journal folder with detailed information.

items.title: What To Do Next
items.content:
Congratulations! You've completed the beginner guide. Here's your path forward to becoming a terminal power user.

You've learned: what a terminal is, how to read the prompt, navigation with {{command}}pwd{{/command}}, {{command}}ls{{/command}}, {{command}}cd{{/command}}, file operations like {{command}}touch{{/command}}, {{command}}nano{{/command}}, {{command}}cat{{/command}}, {{command}}cp{{/command}}, and how to get help.

Now it's time to explore the main course where you'll learn about package management, Git, Python, networking, and much more.
items.example:
{{command}}mkdir challenge{{/command}} - Creates challenge folder.
{{command}}echo 'Done' > done.txt{{/command}} - Creates file with text.
items.exercise: Create a folder called 'challenge' in your home directory. Inside it, create a text file that says 'I completed the beginner guide!' using the echo command. Create a backup copy of that file. List all files in the challenge folder with detailed information to confirm everything is there.

getting-started.title: Getting Started
getting-started.description: Install and set up Termux properly on your device. Get the right version and verify everything works.

items.title: Where to Download Termux
items.content:
The Google Play Store version is abandoned and broken. Always use the F-Droid version for the best experience with regular updates.

F-Droid is an open-source app store that provides the official, maintained version of Termux. The Play Store version was abandoned by the developers and is severely outdated.

After installing from F-Droid, open the app and wait. The first launch takes 10-30 seconds to set up the environment.
items.example: {{command}}pkg --version{{/command}} - Check your Termux version to verify you're on the latest build.
items.exercise: Go to F-Droid on your device. Search for Termux. Check the version number shown. If you have the Play Store version installed, back up your files, uninstall it, and install from F-Droid.

items.title: First Launch and Initial Setup
items.content:
When Termux first opens, you'll see a black screen with white text and a $ symbol. This is your terminal prompt — it means Termux is ready for your commands.

The first thing you should do is update everything. This ensures you have the latest package list and all software is up to date.

Run {{command}}pkg update{{/command}} first to refresh the package list, then {{command}}pkg upgrade{{/command}} to install any updates. When prompted 'Do you want to continue?', type Y and press Enter.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg update{{/command}} - Refreshes package list.
{{command}}pkg upgrade{{/command}} - Installs updates.
items.exercise: Run the command to refresh your package list. Then run the command to upgrade all installed packages. Watch the output carefully to see what's being updated.

items.title: Grant Storage Access
items.content:
Termux needs permission to see your Android files like photos, downloads, and documents. This is essential for working with your phone's files.

Run the {{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} command. Termux will ask for permission to access your storage. Tap 'Allow'.

After this, you'll have access to your Android storage at ~/storage/shared/. This folder is a link to your phone's internal storage.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} - Sets up storage access.
{{command}}ls ~/storage/shared/Download/{{/command}} - Lists Downloads folder.
items.exercise: Run the storage setup command and grant permission when prompted. Navigate to your Downloads folder. List the files there to confirm you can see your Android files.

items.title: Verify Everything Works
items.content:
Run these tests to confirm your Termux installation is working correctly. This will catch any issues early.

Test 1 checks that the package manager works. Test 2 verifies storage access. Test 3 confirms you can create and read files. Test 4 checks your internet connection.

If all tests pass, your Termux is ready for serious work. If any fail, go back and troubleshoot the specific issue.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg --version{{/command}} - Shows version.
{{command}}ls ~/storage/shared/{{/command}} - Lists Android storage.
items.exercise: Run the command to check Termux version. Run the command to list your Android storage. Create a test file and read it back. Test your internet connection by pinging a website. Confirm all four tests pass.

items.title: Understanding Termux Storage
items.content:
Termux has its own private storage separate from Android. This is for security — other apps can't see your Termux files by default.

Your Termux home folder is at /data/data/com.termux/files/home/. This is private to Termux. Other apps on your phone cannot access this folder.

To share files with other apps, you need to copy them to the shared storage at ~/storage/shared/. This folder is accessible by both Termux and Android apps.
items.example: {{command}}cp private.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/{{/command}} - Copies file to shared storage.
items.exercise: Create a file in your Termux home directory. Copy that file to your Android Documents folder. Use your phone's file manager app to verify the file is now visible there.

basic-commands.title: Basic Commands
basic-commands.description: Master the fundamental commands for file management and navigation. These are the commands you'll use every single day.

items.title: pwd - Where Am I?
items.content:
{{command}}pwd{{/command}} stands for Print Working Directory. It shows your exact location in the file system.

Use this command whenever you feel lost. It tells you exactly which folder you're in. This is especially useful when you've been navigating through multiple folders.

If you ever get completely lost, type {{command}}cd ~{{/command}} to go to your home folder, then {{command}}pwd{{/command}} to confirm you're back home.
items.example: {{command}}pwd{{/command}} - Shows current folder path.
items.exercise: Navigate to several different folders. After each move, check your location. Then go to your home folder and confirm you're there.

items.title: ls - What Is Here?
items.content:
{{command}}ls{{/command}} lists all files and folders in your current location. Use it to explore and see what you're working with.

By itself, {{command}}ls{{/command}} shows just the names. Add {{command}}-l{{/command}} for a detailed list with permissions, size, and date. Add {{command}}-a{{/command}} to show hidden files (files starting with a dot).

You can also combine flags: {{command}}ls -la{{/command}} shows everything in long format with hidden files included.
items.example:
{{command}}ls{{/command}} - Basic list.
{{command}}ls -la{{/command}} - Detailed list with hidden files.
items.exercise: Create a few files and a folder. Use the basic list command. Then use the detailed list with permissions. Then include hidden files in your list. Compare the outputs.

items.title: cd - Go There
items.content:
{{command}}cd{{/command}} stands for Change Directory. It moves you into different folders. It's how you navigate the file system.

Use {{command}}cd folder_name{{/command}} to go into a folder. Use {{command}}cd ..{{/command}} to go up one level (to the parent folder). {{command}}cd ~{{/command}} takes you to your home folder from anywhere.

Tab completion is a great time-saver: type {{command}}cd Docu{{/command}} and press Tab — it will auto-complete to {{command}}cd Documents/{{/command}} if that folder exists.
items.example:
{{command}}cd projects/{{/command}} - Goes into projects folder.
{{command}}cd ..{{/command}} - Goes up one level.
items.exercise: Navigate to the root directory. Then go to your home folder. Then go into a subfolder. Then go up one level. Use the tab completion feature to navigate to a folder.

items.title: mkdir - Create Folders
items.content:
{{command}}mkdir{{/command}} stands for Make Directory. It creates new folders to organize your files.

Always use lowercase names without spaces for compatibility. Use underscores or hyphens instead of spaces: my_folder or my-folder.

You can create multiple folders at once by listing them all after the command.
items.example:
{{command}}mkdir projects{{/command}} - Creates a folder.
{{command}}mkdir web mobile{{/command}} - Creates two folders.
items.exercise: Create a main folder. Then create multiple subfolders inside it at once. Use the recursive list command to verify your folder structure.

items.title: touch - Create Empty Files
items.content:
{{command}}touch{{/command}} creates an empty file. It's also used to update a file's timestamp to the current time.

If the file doesn't exist, {{command}}touch{{/command}} creates it. If it already exists, {{command}}touch{{/command}} updates its modification time without changing the content.

You can create multiple files at once by listing all their names.
items.example:
{{command}}touch file.txt{{/command}} - Creates empty file.
{{command}}touch file1.txt file2.txt{{/command}} - Creates two files.
items.exercise: Create several empty files. Check their timestamps. Then use touch on one file to update its timestamp. Verify the timestamp changed.

items.title: cat - Read Files
items.content:
{{command}}cat{{/command}} displays the entire contents of a file. It's great for small files but can overwhelm your screen for large ones.

For large files, use {{command}}less{{/command}} to scroll through page by page, {{command}}head{{/command}} to see the first few lines, or {{command}}tail{{/command}} to see the last few lines.

{{command}}cat{{/command}} can also combine multiple files: {{command}}cat file1.txt file2.txt{{/command}} shows both one after another.
items.example:
{{command}}cat notes.txt{{/command}} - Shows entire file.
{{command}}head -3 notes.txt{{/command}} - Shows first 3 lines.
items.exercise: Create a file with multiple lines of text. View the entire file. Then view only the first few lines. Then view only the last few lines.

items.title: cp - Copy Files
items.content:
{{command}}cp{{/command}} stands for Copy. It creates a copy of a file or folder. The original remains unchanged, and you get a duplicate.

To copy a folder and everything inside it, use {{command}}-r{{/command}} (recursive). To preserve timestamps and permissions, use {{command}}-p{{/command}}.

Copying is safe — it never changes the original file. Use it for backups or creating new versions.
items.example:
{{command}}cp file.txt backup.txt{{/command}} - Copies file.
{{command}}cp -r project/ project-backup/{{/command}} - Copies folder.
items.exercise: Create a file with some content. Copy it to a new name. Verify both files exist. Then copy the file to a different folder.

items.title: mv - Move or Rename
items.content:
{{command}}mv{{/command}} stands for Move. It moves files to different locations OR renames them. Unlike {{command}}cp{{/command}}, no copy is created — the file actually moves.

When you use {{command}}mv{{/command}} to rename a file, it stays in the same folder but gets a new name. When you use it to move a file, it goes to a different folder.

The difference from {{command}}cp{{/command}}: {{command}}cp{{/command}} makes a duplicate, {{command}}mv{{/command}} actually moves the file (no copy remains in the original location).
items.example:
{{command}}mv oldname.txt newname.txt{{/command}} - Renames file.
{{command}}mv file.txt ~/Documents/{{/command}} - Moves file.
items.exercise: Create a file. Rename it. Then move it to a different folder. Verify the original location is now empty and the file is in the new location.

items.title: rm - Delete Files
items.content:
{{command}}rm{{/command}} stands for Remove. It permanently deletes files. There is NO undo — be very careful with this command.

Always use {{command}}-i{{/command}} (interactive) when learning — it asks for confirmation before deleting each file. Use {{command}}ls{{/command}} first to see what you're deleting before running {{command}}rm{{/command}}.

Never run {{command}}rm -rf /{{/command}} — this would delete everything in Termux. Be extremely careful with recursive deletion ({{command}}-r{{/command}}) and force ({{command}}-f{{/command}}) flags.
items.example:
{{command}}rm -i file.txt{{/command}} - Deletes with confirmation.
{{command}}rm *.txt{{/command}} - Deletes all .txt files.
items.exercise: Create several test files. Delete one file with confirmation. Delete the remaining files all at once. Use ls to verify the files are gone.

items.title: echo - Print Text
items.content:
{{command}}echo{{/command}} prints text to the screen. It's one of the simplest commands but also one of the most useful for scripting and testing.

You can use {{command}}echo{{/command}} to display messages, check environment variables, or create files with content using redirection.

When combined with {{command}}> {{/command}} (redirection), {{command}}echo{{/command}} can write content directly to a file, creating it if it doesn't exist.
items.example:
{{command}}echo 'Hello World'{{/command}} - Prints message.
{{command}}echo 'Hello' > file.txt{{/command}} - Writes to file.
items.exercise: Print a message to the screen. Print the value of the HOME environment variable. Create a file with content using echo and redirection.

file-system.title: File System
file-system.description: Understand the Termux file system structure and paths. Knowing where things are and how paths work is essential.

items.title: Termux Directory Structure
items.content:
Termux has its own isolated file system. Understanding where things are helps you navigate efficiently.

Your home folder (~) is where all your personal files and projects should go. This is the default location when you open Termux.

The packages folder ($PREFIX) is where installed software lives. You rarely need to touch this.

After running {{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}}, you can access your Android storage at ~/storage/shared/.
items.example:
{{command}}cd ~{{/command}} - Goes to home.
{{command}}cd $PREFIX{{/command}} - Goes to packages folder.
items.exercise: Navigate to each of these folders and use ls to see what's inside: home, packages folder, and Android storage.

items.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
items.content:
Paths tell the computer where a file is. Understanding the difference is crucial for navigating efficiently.

An absolute path starts from the root (/) and works no matter where you are. Example: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/practice/mynote.txt

A relative path starts from your current location. Example: practice/mynote.txt (only works if you're in the home folder).

Special shortcuts: . (current folder), .. (parent folder), ~ (home folder), - (previous folder).
items.example:
{{command}}cd /data/data/com.termux/files/home{{/command}} - Absolute path.
{{command}}cd ~{{/command}} - Relative shortcut.
items.exercise: Navigate using absolute path. Then navigate using relative path. Use pwd to verify your location each time.

items.title: Viewing Files with less and head/tail
items.content:
For large files, cat is not practical. Use less, head, and tail instead.

less lets you scroll through a file page by page. Use Space for next page, b for previous, q to quit, and / to search.

head shows the beginning of a file (first 10 lines by default). tail shows the end (last 10 lines by default). Use -n to specify a different number of lines.
items.example:
{{command}}less file.txt{{/command}} - Scroll through file.
{{command}}head -20 file.txt{{/command}} - Shows first 20 lines.
items.exercise: Create a file with 50 lines of text. Use head, tail, and less to view different parts of it.

storage-access.title: Storage Access
storage-access.description: Access and manage files on your Android device from Termux. This covers setting up storage access and working with Android files.

items.title: Setting Up Storage Access
items.content:
Before you can access your Android files, you need to run {{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}}. This command requests permission to access your phone's storage.

After you grant permission, you'll have access to your Android storage through ~/storage/. You'll see folders like shared/, downloads/, dcim/, pictures/, music/, and movies/.

If storage doesn't work properly, try removing the storage folder and setting it up again with {{command}}rm -rf ~/storage && termux-setup-storage{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} - Sets up storage.
{{command}}ls ~/storage/{{/command}} - Lists storage folders.
items.exercise: Run the storage setup command and grant permission. Navigate to Downloads and list the files to confirm access.

items.title: Accessing Android Folders
items.content:
After setup, your Android storage is accessible through ~/storage/. Each folder maps to a different part of your Android storage.

~/storage/shared/ is the root of your internal storage. The shortcuts like downloads/, dcim/, pictures/, music/, movies/, and documents/ give you quick access to specific folders.

You can navigate to these folders, list files, copy, move, and delete files just like any other folder in Termux.
items.example:
{{command}}cd ~/storage/shared/Downloads{{/command}} - Goes to Downloads.
{{command}}ls ~/storage/shared/DCIM/Camera/{{/command}} - Lists camera photos.
items.exercise: Navigate to your Downloads folder and list the files. Copy a file from there to your Termux home folder. Then navigate to your DCIM folder and list the photos there.

items.title: Moving Files Between Environments
items.example:
{{command}}cp myfile.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/{{/command}} - Copies to Android.
{{command}}mv ~/storage/shared/Download/file.pdf ~/{{/command}} - Moves to Termux.
items.exercise: Create a file in Termux. Copy it to your Android Documents folder. Verify it appears there. Then move a file from Android to Termux.

items.title: Working with External SD Cards
items.content:
If your device has an SD card, you can access it from Termux. The location varies by device.

Common SD card mount points are /storage/sdcard1/ or /storage/XXXX-XXXX/ (where XXXX is a long alphanumeric string).

You can create a symlink for easier access: {{command}}ln -s /storage/sdcard1 ~/sdcard{{/command}}. Then you can just use {{command}}cd ~/sdcard{{/command}} to access your SD card.
items.example:
{{command}}ls /storage/{{/command}} - Lists storage devices.
{{command}}ln -s /storage/sdcard1 ~/sdcard{{/command}} - Creates symlink.
items.exercise: Check if you have an SD card mounted. If found, create a symlink for easier access and navigate to it.

package-management.title: Package Management
package-management.description: Learn to install and manage software packages on Termux. Package management is how you get new tools and keep everything up to date.

items.title: What is a Package Manager?
items.content:
A package manager is like an app store for the command line. It downloads, installs, and manages software automatically.

Termux uses {{command}}pkg{{/command}} as its package manager. When you tell it what to install, it handles everything: finding the software, downloading it, installing dependencies, and setting it up correctly.

The benefits are huge: automatic dependency handling, easy updates for all software, clean uninstallation, and verified safe packages from trusted repositories.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg install python{{/command}} - Installs Python.
{{command}}pkg uninstall python{{/command}} - Removes Python.
items.exercise: Search for a package related to Python. Install the nano text editor if you don't have it. List all the packages you have installed.

items.title: Essential pkg Commands
items.content:
These are the only {{command}}pkg{{/command}} commands you need to know. Memorize them and you can manage any package.

Always start with {{command}}pkg update{{/command}} to refresh the list of available packages, then {{command}}pkg upgrade{{/command}} to install updates. This should be your first action whenever you open Termux.

Use {{command}}pkg search{{/command}} to find packages, {{command}}pkg install{{/command}} to install them, and {{command}}pkg uninstall{{/command}} to remove them.

The {{command}}pkg clean{{/command}} command removes downloaded package files, which frees up space on your device.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg search htop{{/command}} - Searches for htop.
{{command}}pkg install htop{{/command}} - Installs it.
items.exercise: Refresh your package list. Search for a package called 'htop'. Install it. Run it and press Q to quit. Uninstall it. Clean up downloaded package files.

items.title: Must-Have Packages
items.content:
These packages are essential for any Termux user. Install them to unlock the full potential of your terminal.

Text editors: {{command}}nano{{/command}} and {{command}}vim{{/command}}. File downloading: {{command}}wget{{/command}} and {{command}}curl{{/command}}. Programming: {{command}}python{{/command}} and {{command}}nodejs{{/command}}. Version control: {{command}}git{{/command}}. System access: {{command}}openssh{{/command}}. Utilities: {{command}}tree{{/command}}, {{command}}htop{{/command}}, and {{command}}man{{/command}}.
items.example: {{command}}pkg install tree htop man{{/command}} - Installs multiple packages at once.
items.exercise: Install the tree package and use it to visualize your home folder structure. Install htop and run it to see your system processes. Install the manual pages system and read the manual for a command.

items.title: Repository Management
items.content:
Packages come from repositories. You can change mirrors if downloads are slow or add extra repositories for more software.

Termux has several repositories: main (primary), root (for rooted devices), x11 (graphical applications), and game (games).

Use {{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} to switch to a faster mirror if downloads are slow. Use arrow keys to navigate, Space to select, Enter to confirm.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} - Opens mirror selector.
{{command}}cat $PREFIX/etc/apt/sources.list{{/command}} - Shows current repos.
items.exercise: Run the repository change tool to see the available mirrors. View your current repository list to see where your packages come from.

items.title: Working with Different Package Sources
items.content:
Not all software is in Termux repositories. Here is how to get software from other sources.

Python packages can be installed with pip. Node.js packages with npm. Ruby gems with gem.

You can also build software from source when packages aren't available in the repositories.
items.example:
{{command}}pip install requests{{/command}} - Installs Python package.
{{command}}npm install -g nodemon{{/command}} - Installs Node package.
items.exercise: Install a Python package using pip. Then install a Node.js package using npm.

git-github.title: Git & GitHub
git-github.description: Learn version control with Git and collaborate on GitHub. Git is essential for any developer, and GitHub is where you'll share your work.

items.title: Installing and Configuring Git
items.content:
Git tracks changes to files. Think of it as an unlimited undo button for your code and documents.

First, install Git with {{command}}pkg install git{{/command}}. Then configure your identity with {{command}}git config --global user.name{{/command}} and {{command}}git config --global user.email{{/command}}. This information is attached to every commit you make.

Set your default editor to nano with {{command}}git config --global core.editor 'nano'{{/command}} for an easier experience.
items.example:
{{command}}git config --global user.name 'Jane Doe'{{/command}} - Sets your name.
{{command}}git config --global user.email 'jane@email.com'{{/command}} - Sets your email.
items.exercise: Install Git. Configure your name and email. Set nano as your default editor. Verify your configuration is correct.

items.title: Basic Git Workflow
items.content:
This is the standard workflow you'll use 90% of the time with Git. Master this and you master version control.

Start with {{command}}git init{{/command}} to create a repository. Make changes to your files, then use {{command}}git status{{/command}} to see what changed. Stage changes with {{command}}git add{{/command}}, then commit them with a message describing what you did.

Use {{command}}git log{{/command}} to see the history of your commits. Connect to a remote repository with {{command}}git remote add{{/command}} and push your changes with {{command}}git push{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}git init{{/command}} - Creates a repository.
{{command}}git add file.txt{{/command}} - Stages a file.
{{command}}git commit -m 'Message'{{/command}} - Commits with message.
items.exercise: Create a new project folder and initialize Git. Create a file and add content to it. Stage the file. Commit it with a message. View your commit history.

items.title: Understanding Branches
items.content:
Branches let you work on different features separately. The main branch (often called main or master) is the stable version.

Create a new branch with {{command}}git branch feature-name{{/command}} and switch to it with {{command}}git checkout feature-name{{/command}}. Or do both at once with {{command}}git checkout -b feature-name{{/command}}.

When your feature is ready, merge it back to main with {{command}}git merge feature-name{{/command}}. Delete the branch with {{command}}git branch -d feature-name{{/command}} when you're done.
items.example:
{{command}}git checkout -b new-feature{{/command}} - Creates and switches branch.
{{command}}git merge new-feature{{/command}} - Merges branch into current.
items.exercise: Create a new branch and switch to it. Make a change to your file. Switch back to main. Merge your changes from the branch. Delete the branch.

items.title: Working with GitHub
items.content:
Clone repositories to get code from GitHub and contribute to open source projects.

To clone a repository, use {{command}}git clone https://github.com/user/repository.git{{/command}}. This downloads the entire repository to your device.

For SSH access, generate an SSH key with {{command}}ssh-keygen -t ed25519{{/command}}, then add the public key to your GitHub account. This allows passwordless pushes and pulls.
items.example:
{{command}}git clone https://github.com/octocat/Hello-World.git{{/command}} - Clones repository.
{{command}}ssh-keygen -t ed25519{{/command}} - Generates SSH key.
items.exercise: Generate an SSH key pair. View your public key. Add it to your GitHub account under SSH keys. Clone a public repository from GitHub.

items.title: Undoing Changes
items.content:
Fix mistakes and revert changes in Git. There are several ways to undo depending on what you need.

To unstage a file: {{command}}git reset HEAD file.txt{{/command}}. To discard changes to a file: {{command}}git checkout -- file.txt{{/command}}.

To undo the last commit keeping changes: {{command}}git reset --soft HEAD~1{{/command}}. To undo the last commit discarding changes: {{command}}git reset --hard HEAD~1{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}git reset HEAD file.txt{{/command}} - Unstages file.
{{command}}git checkout -- file.txt{{/command}} - Discards changes.
items.exercise: Make some commits, then practice undoing changes using the different methods: unstage a file, discard changes to a file, and undo the last commit.

networking.title: Networking & SSH
networking.description: Connect to other computers and transfer files securely. SSH is the standard for remote access, and mastering it opens up a world of possibilities.

items.title: SSH Client
items.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) lets you securely connect to and control other computers. It's the standard for remote server access.

To connect, use {{command}}ssh username@hostname_or_ip{{/command}}. For example, {{command}}ssh user@192.168.1.100{{/command}} connects to a computer on your local network.

Use {{command}}-p{{/command}} to specify a different port (default is 22). Use {{command}}-i{{/command}} to specify a private key file.
items.example:
{{command}}ssh user@192.168.1.100{{/command}} - Connects to remote computer.
{{command}}ssh -p 2222 user@server.com{{/command}} - Connects on custom port.
items.exercise: If you have another computer on your network, try connecting to it via SSH. If you don't, research how to set up a local SSH server for practice. Once connected, run a few commands on the remote machine.

items.title: SSH Server (Access Your Phone)
items.content:
Turn your phone into an SSH server and access it from your computer or another device.

Start the server with {{command}}sshd{{/command}}. It runs on port 8022 (not 22, because Android restricts low ports).

Find your phone's IP address with {{command}}ifconfig{{/command}} or {{command}}ip addr show | grep inet{{/command}}. Then connect from your computer with {{command}}ssh -p 8022 username@phone_ip{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}sshd{{/command}} - Starts SSH server.
{{command}}ssh -p 8022 user@192.168.1.105{{/command}} - Connects to phone.
items.exercise: Start the SSH server on your phone. Find your phone's IP address. From your computer, connect to your phone using SSH. Run commands on your phone from your computer.

items.title: File Transfer with SCP and Rsync
items.example:
{{command}}scp -P 8022 user@192.168.1.105:~/notes.txt ./{{/command}} - Copies from phone.
{{command}}rsync -avz -e 'ssh -p 8022' user@phone:~/docs/ ./backup/{{/command}} - Syncs folder.
items.exercise: Copy a file from your phone to your computer using SCP. Then copy it back. Then install rsync and sync a folder between your phone and computer.

items.title: Network Tools
items.content:
Useful commands for testing connectivity and network diagnostics.

{{command}}ping{{/command}} tests connectivity. {{command}}wget{{/command}} and {{command}}curl{{/command}} download files. {{command}}nmap{{/command}} scans ports. {{command}}traceroute{{/command}} traces network paths. {{command}}dig{{/command}} and {{command}}nslookup{{/command}} perform DNS lookups.
items.example:
{{command}}ping -c 4 google.com{{/command}} - Tests connectivity.
{{command}}curl ifconfig.me{{/command}} - Shows public IP.
items.exercise: Test connectivity to a website. Download a small file from the internet. Check your public IP address. Trace the network path to google.com.

python-dev.title: Python Development
python-dev.description: Write and run Python code on your Android device. Python is one of the most popular languages for beginners and professionals.

items.title: Installing Python
items.content:
Python is a beginner-friendly programming language that's perfect for scripting and automation on Termux.

Install Python with {{command}}pkg install python{{/command}}. Verify the installation with {{command}}python --version{{/command}}.

Pip is Python's package manager. Upgrade it with {{command}}pip install --upgrade pip{{/command}}.

You can run Python interactively with {{command}}python{{/command}} (the REPL), or run a script with {{command}}python my_script.py{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}python --version{{/command}} - Shows Python version.
{{command}}python{{/command}} - Starts interactive interpreter.
items.exercise: Install Python. Verify it's installed correctly. Start the Python interpreter and print 'Hello World'. Exit the interpreter. Create a Python script file and run it.

items.title: Installing Python Packages
items.content:
Python has thousands of packages for everything from web development to data science. Use pip to install them.

Install a package with {{command}}pip install package_name{{/command}}. You can install multiple packages at once.

List installed packages with {{command}}pip list{{/command}}. Show details with {{command}}pip show package_name{{/command}}.

Save your dependencies to a file with {{command}}pip freeze > requirements.txt{{/command}} and install from that file with {{command}}pip install -r requirements.txt{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}pip install requests{{/command}} - Installs requests.
{{command}}pip freeze > requirements.txt{{/command}} - Saves dependencies.
items.exercise: Install the requests package. Create a Python script that downloads a webpage. Save your installed packages to a requirements file.

items.title: Creating a Simple Web Server
items.content:
Start a web server in one line of Python. This is great for sharing files or testing web development.

Use Python's built-in HTTP server: {{command}}python -m http.server 8000{{/command}}. This serves the current directory on port 8000.

You can specify a different directory: {{command}}python -m http.server 8000 --directory /sdcard/Download{{/command}}.

For more flexibility, use Flask: install it with {{command}}pip install flask{{/command}}, then create a simple app.
items.example:
{{command}}python -m http.server 8000{{/command}} - Starts web server.
{{command}}python -m http.server 8000 --directory /sdcard/Download{{/command}} - Serves Downloads folder.
items.exercise: Start a web server serving your current folder. Open your browser to see your files. Stop the server. Start a server serving your Downloads folder instead.

items.title: Working with APIs
items.content:
Fetch data from internet APIs using Python. This is how you interact with web services programmatically.

Install the requests library: {{command}}pip install requests{{/command}}. Then use it in your Python scripts to make HTTP requests.

APIs return data in JSON format which you can parse and use in your applications.
items.example: {{command}}import requests; requests.get('https://api.example.com/data'){{/command}} - Fetches API data.
items.exercise: Install the requests library. Write a Python script that fetches data from a public API and prints the response.

node-dev.title: Node.js Development
node-dev.description: Build JavaScript applications with Node.js on Termux. Node.js is the runtime that powers modern web development.

items.title: Installing Node.js
items.content:
Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside of a browser. It's essential for modern web development and JavaScript tooling.

Install Node.js with {{command}}pkg install nodejs{{/command}}. Verify with {{command}}node --version{{/command}} and {{command}}npm --version{{/command}}.

NPM is Node's package manager. You can run Node interactively with {{command}}node{{/command}} (the REPL), or run a script with {{command}}node app.js{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}node --version{{/command}} - Shows Node version.
{{command}}node{{/command}} - Starts REPL.
items.exercise: Install Node.js. Verify it's installed correctly. Start the REPL and run a simple JavaScript command. Create a script file and run it.

items.title: Creating a Web Server with Express
items.content:
Express is the most popular Node.js web framework. It makes building web servers simple and fast.

Create a new project folder and initialize npm with {{command}}npm init -y{{/command}}. Install Express with {{command}}npm install express{{/command}}.

Create a server.js file with a basic Express server. Run it with {{command}}node server.js{{/command}} or use nodemon for auto-restart.
items.example:
{{command}}npm init -y{{/command}} - Initializes project.
{{command}}npm install express{{/command}} - Installs Express.
items.exercise: Create a project folder and initialize npm. Install Express. Create a server file that responds with 'Hello World'. Run it and test it in your browser.

items.title: Useful npm Packages
items.content:
Install global tools and local packages for development. Global packages are installed with {{command}}-g{{/command}} and are available everywhere.

Useful global packages: {{command}}nodemon{{/command}} (auto-restart server), {{command}}pm2{{/command}} (process manager), {{command}}http-server{{/command}} (simple HTTP server).

Local packages: {{command}}axios{{/command}} (HTTP client), {{command}}chalk{{/command}} (colored output), {{command}}dotenv{{/command}} (environment variables).
items.example:
{{command}}npm install -g http-server{{/command}} - Installs globally.
{{command}}npm install chalk{{/command}} - Installs locally.
items.exercise: Install http-server globally and use it to serve a directory. Install chalk locally and use it in a script to print colored output.

customization.title: Customization
customization.description: Make Termux look and feel the way you want. Customize your shell, colors, and shortcuts for a better experience.

items.title: Zsh and Oh My Zsh
items.content:
Upgrade from Bash to Zsh with themes and plugins. Zsh offers better auto-completion, theming, and plugins.

Install Zsh with {{command}}pkg install zsh{{/command}}, then change your default shell with {{command}}chsh -s zsh{{/command}}. Restart Termux for the change to take effect.

Install Oh My Zsh for easy theming: {{command}}sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)"{{/command}}. Change your theme by editing ~/.zshrc.
items.example:
{{command}}chsh -s zsh{{/command}} - Changes default shell.
{{command}}source ~/.zshrc{{/command}} - Reloads config.
items.exercise: Install Zsh. Change your default shell to Zsh. Restart Termux. Install Oh My Zsh. Change your theme to something you like. Apply the changes.

items.title: Color Schemes
items.content:
Customize terminal colors by editing colors.properties. You can create your own theme or use a pre-made one.

Create the .termux directory if it doesn't exist: {{command}}mkdir -p ~/.termux{{/command}}.

Edit colors.properties with {{command}}nano ~/.termux/colors.properties{{/command}}. Add your color settings like background, foreground, cursor, and palette colors.

Restart Termux to apply your new color scheme.
items.example:
{{command}}mkdir -p ~/.termux{{/command}} - Creates directory.
{{command}}nano ~/.termux/colors.properties{{/command}} - Opens color file.
items.exercise: Create the .termux directory if needed. Open the colors file and add a custom color scheme. Save and restart Termux to see your new colors.

items.title: Font Size and Style
items.content:
Adjust font size on the fly and change the font family.

Volume Up button increases font size. Volume Down button decreases font size.

To change the font family, edit termux.properties and add a font path.
items.example:
{{command}}nano ~/.termux/termux.properties{{/command}} - Opens settings file.
{{command}}font = /path/to/font.ttf{{/command}} - Changes font.
items.exercise: Use the volume keys to change font size. Then change the font family in termux.properties.

items.title: Custom Aliases
items.content:
Create shortcuts for frequently used commands. Aliases save time and reduce typos.

Edit your shell configuration file (~/.zshrc for Zsh, ~/.bashrc for Bash). Add alias definitions like {{command}}alias ll='ls -la'{{/command}}.

After adding aliases, reload your config with {{command}}source ~/.zshrc{{/command}} (or source ~/.bashrc).
items.example:
{{command}}alias ll='ls -la'{{/command}} - Creates alias.
{{command}}source ~/.zshrc{{/command}} - Reloads config.
items.exercise: Add aliases for ls -la, for updating packages, and for going to your home folder. Reload your configuration. Test each alias to make sure it works.

shortcuts.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
shortcuts.description: Speed up your workflow with essential keyboard shortcuts. Learning shortcuts saves time and makes you more efficient.

items.title: Essential Terminal Shortcuts
items.content:
These shortcuts work in almost every terminal environment. Learn them to navigate and edit faster.

Ctrl+C stops the current process. Ctrl+D exits the current shell. Ctrl+L clears the screen.

Ctrl+A jumps to the beginning of the line, Ctrl+E jumps to the end. Ctrl+U deletes to the beginning, Ctrl+K deletes to the end.

Up/Down arrows navigate command history. Tab auto-completes commands and filenames.
items.example:
Ctrl+C - Stops process.
Ctrl+L - Clears screen.
Ctrl+A - Goes to start of line.
items.exercise: Type a long command. Use the shortcuts to jump to the beginning and end of the line. Delete to the beginning and to the end. Use the up arrow to recall previous commands.

items.title: Termux-Specific Shortcuts
items.content:
Termux uses volume keys because Android keyboards lack certain keys like Ctrl, Alt, and Escape.

Volume Up + Q = Ctrl key. Volume Up + W = Tilde (~). Volume Up + E = Pipe (|). Volume Up + R = Backslash (\)

Volume Down + D = Escape key. Volume Down + L = Tab key. Volume Down + K = Delete key.

You can also add a permanent extra keys row with 'extra-keys' in termux.properties.
items.example:
Volume Up + Q - Sends Ctrl.
Volume Up + E - Types |.
Volume Down + D - Sends Escape.
items.exercise: Try the Volume Up shortcuts for Ctrl, pipe, and tilde. Then add an extra keys row with ESC, CTRL, ALT, and arrow keys. Reload Termux settings.

items.title: Nano Text Editor Shortcuts
items.content:
^ means Ctrl (so ^O means press Ctrl and O together). These shortcuts make editing in Nano fast and efficient.

^O saves the file (Write Out). ^X exits Nano. ^K cuts the current line. ^U pastes (Uncut) the cut line.

^W searches for text. ^\ searches and replaces. ^G shows help. ^C shows cursor position.

Alt+U undoes, Alt+E redoes. Alt+A selects text, Alt+6 copies the selected text.
items.example:
^O - Saves file.
^X - Exits Nano.
^K - Cuts line.
^U - Pastes line.
items.exercise: Open a file in Nano. Practice saving, searching, cutting, and pasting. Enable line numbers in your Nano configuration.

items.title: Vim Text Editor Shortcuts
items.content:
Vim is a powerful text editor with a steeper learning curve. Here are the basics to get you started.

Modes: i (Insert mode), Esc (Normal mode), v (Visual mode).

In Normal mode: :w saves, :q quits, :wq saves and quits, :q! quits without saving.

Movement: h (left), j (down), k (up), l (right). 0 (start of line), $ (end of line), gg (start of file), G (end of file).

Editing: x (delete character), dd (delete line), yy (copy line), p (paste below).
items.example:
:w - Saves file.
:q - Quits.
i - Enters Insert mode.
Esc - Returns to Normal mode.
items.exercise: Install vim with pkg install vim. Open a file, practice entering Insert mode, saving, and exiting. Try moving around with h, j, k, l.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.description: Fix common issues and errors in Termux. Knowing how to troubleshoot saves time and frustration.

items.title: Repository Errors
items.content:
If {{command}}pkg update{{/command}} fails, try these solutions.

First, change the repository mirror with {{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} and select a different mirror.

If that doesn't work, clear the cache with {{command}}pkg clean{{/command}} and try again. You can also reset repositories by removing the lists folder.

Check your internet connection with {{command}}ping google.com{{/command}} and verify your date/time settings are correct.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} - Changes mirror.
{{command}}pkg clean{{/command}} - Clears cache.
items.exercise: Run the repository change tool and explore the available mirrors. Clear the package cache. Test your internet connection with ping.

items.title: Storage Permission Issues
items.content:
If you cannot access Android files, fix storage permissions.

Re-run {{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} to request permission again. Check Android Settings to ensure Termux has Storage permission.

On Android 11+, you may need to enable 'Allow management of all files' in the permissions settings.

You can also manually recreate the symlinks by removing ~/storage and running {{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} again.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-setup-storage{{/command}} - Requests storage permission.
{{command}}rm -rf ~/storage && termux-setup-storage{{/command}} - Recreates symlinks.
items.exercise: Check your storage permissions in Android Settings. Run the storage setup command again. If it doesn't work, remove the storage folder and run setup again.

items.title: Package Installation Failures
items.content:
When {{command}}pkg install{{/command}} fails, use these fixes.

First, update everything with {{command}}pkg update && pkg upgrade{{/command}}. Then clear the cache with {{command}}pkg clean{{/command}}.

Check your disk space with {{command}}df -h{{/command}} — you might need to free up space. Try reinstalling the package with {{command}}pkg reinstall <package>{{/command}}.

If dependencies are broken, run {{command}}pkg install -f{{/command}} to fix them. Also verify that the package exists with {{command}}pkg search <package-name>{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg update && pkg upgrade{{/command}} - Updates everything.
{{command}}pkg install -f{{/command}} - Fixes dependencies.
items.exercise: Check your available disk space. Clean the package cache. Try installing a package. If it fails, try fixing dependencies.

items.title: Termux Won't Start or Keeps Crashing
items.content:
If Termux crashes on launch, try these solutions.

First, clear the cache in Android Settings. If that doesn't work, clear all data (this will delete everything in Termux).

You can also reinstall Termux from F-Droid. Backup your files first.

Disable battery optimization for Termux and make sure you're using the F-Droid version.
items.example:
Settings > Apps > Termux > Storage > Clear Cache - Clears cache.
Settings > Apps > Termux > Storage > Clear Data - Clears all data.
items.exercise: If Termux is crashing, clear the cache first. If that doesn't work, backup your files and clear data or reinstall.

items.title: SSH Connection Issues
items.content:
Fix problems when connecting via SSH.

First, check if {{command}}sshd{{/command}} is running with {{command}}ps aux | grep sshd{{/command}}. If not, start it with {{command}}sshd{{/command}}.

Verify you're using the correct port (8022) and the correct IP address. Both devices must be on the same network.

Check permissions on ~/.ssh (should be 700) and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (should be 600).

Regenerate SSH keys if needed and check the SSH logs with {{command}}logcat -s Termux:SSH{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}ps aux | grep sshd{{/command}} - Checks if running.
{{command}}chmod 700 ~/.ssh{{/command}} - Fixes permissions.
items.exercise: Start the SSH server. Check if it's running. Find your IP address. Check your SSH permissions. If you have issues, view the SSH logs.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.description: Common questions and answers about Termux. Find answers to the most frequently asked questions.

items.title: Do I need root access?
items.content:
No. Termux works perfectly without root. The vast majority of features work without any root access at all.

Root access is only needed for certain advanced features like running root-only tools or modifying system files. For everyday use, learning, and development, root is not required.
items.example: Installing packages, writing scripts, navigating the file system, and using tools like Git and Python all work perfectly without root.
items.exercise: Try using Termux without root. Install a package, create files, navigate folders. You'll find everything works perfectly.

items.title: Play Store vs F-Droid?
items.content:
Always use the F-Droid version. The Play Store version is no longer maintained and has serious issues.

The Play Store version is years behind and broken. The F-Droid version is actively maintained, receives regular updates, and has all the latest features and security fixes.
items.example: The F-Droid version has a version number like 0.118.0. The Play Store version is stuck on much older versions.
items.exercise: Check which version you have installed. If it's from Play Store, back up your files, uninstall it, and install from F-Droid.

items.title: How to backup my Termux setup?
items.content:
Backup your home directory and list of installed packages.

Use tar to create a backup of your home folder. Save the list of installed packages to a file.

Copy both files to your Android shared storage for safe keeping.
items.example:
{{command}}tar -czf termux-backup.tar.gz ~/{{/command}} - Creates backup.
{{command}}pkg list-installed > packages.txt{{/command}} - Saves package list.
items.exercise: Create a backup of your Termux home folder. Save a list of installed packages. Copy both files to your Android storage.

items.title: How to prevent Android from killing Termux?
items.content:
Android may terminate background apps to save battery. Here's how to prevent it.

Disable battery optimization for Termux in Android Settings. Use {{command}}termux-wake-lock{{/command}} to keep Termux awake. Keep Termux in the foreground by running a long-running command.

You can also lock Termux in the recents view by opening the recent apps and tapping the lock icon.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-wake-lock{{/command}} - Prevents sleep.
Settings > Apps > Termux > Battery > Unrestricted - Disables optimization.
items.exercise: Check your battery optimization settings for Termux. Install termux-api and use the wake lock. Lock Termux in the recent apps view.

items.title: Can I run GUI applications?
items.content:
Yes, you can run basic GUI applications using VNC or Termux:X11.

Termux:X11 is a native Android app that provides an X11 server for running GUI apps. You need to install it from F-Droid.

VNC is another option. Install tigervnc, start the server with {{command}}vncserver{{/command}}, and connect with a VNC viewer app to localhost:5901.
items.example:
{{command}}vncserver{{/command}} - Starts VNC server.
{{command}}vncserver -kill :1{{/command}} - Stops it.
items.exercise: Install tigervnc. Start a VNC server. Connect to it with a VNC viewer app. Install a GUI package and launch it through VNC.

items.title: How to change the default shell?
items.content:
The default shell is Bash. You can switch to Zsh for more features like better auto-completion and theming.

Install Zsh with {{command}}pkg install zsh{{/command}}, then change your default shell with {{command}}chsh -s zsh{{/command}}. Restart Termux for the change to take effect.

To change back to Bash, run {{command}}chsh -s bash{{/command}}. You can see available shells with {{command}}cat /etc/shells{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}chsh -s zsh{{/command}} - Changes to Zsh.
{{command}}chsh -s bash{{/command}} - Changes back to Bash.
items.exercise: Install Zsh. Change your default shell to Zsh. Restart Termux. See available shells. Change back to Bash if you prefer.

items.title: How to update Termux itself?
items.content:
Termux is updated through F-Droid, not through pkg.

To update the Termux app, open F-Droid and go to Settings > Updates. Or download the latest APK from F-Droid.

To update packages inside Termux, run {{command}}pkg update && pkg upgrade{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}pkg --version{{/command}} - Shows Termux version.
Open F-Droid to check for app updates.
items.exercise: Check your Termux version. Check F-Droid for app updates. Update your packages inside Termux.

items.title: How to fix 'Cannot connect to repository' error?
items.content:
This usually means your repository mirror is down.

Quick fix: {{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} and select a different mirror.

If that fails: {{command}}pkg clean{{/command}} and {{command}}rm -rf $PREFIX/var/lib/apt/lists/*{{/command}} then {{command}}pkg update{{/command}}.
items.example:
{{command}}termux-change-repo{{/command}} - Changes mirror.
{{command}}rm -rf $PREFIX/var/lib/apt/lists/*{{/command}} - Resets repositories.
items.exercise: Change your repository mirror using termux-change-repo. If it doesn't work, reset your repositories and try again.

items.title: How to access Termux from PC without USB?
items.example:
{{command}}ssh -p 8022 user@192.168.1.105{{/command}} - Connects from PC.
{{command}}scp -P 8022 file.txt user@phone:~/.{{/command}} - Transfers file.
items.exercise: Install openssh and start the server. Find your phone's IP. Connect from your computer. Set up passwordless login with SSH keys.
